newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany unlikely to hit deficit criteria in 97.
newsitem.headline: Germany unlikely to hit deficit criteria in 97.

text.p: Germany is unlikely to meet the Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria in 1997 but should still be among the first group of nations to join Europe's currency union, a Bundesbank council member said on Friday.

"I share doubts that Germany can reach the (three percent) reference value on the budget deficit ratio as compared with gross domestic product (in 1997)," Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told the Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper.
Germany unlikely to hit deficit criteria in 97
But in the interview, slated to be published in the newspaper's Saturday edition, Welteke suggested that Germany would not be excluded from adopting the new currency, euro, in 1999.

"Contrary to impressions which often arise in Germany, three percent is not a 'knock out criteria,'" Welteke said, stressing the Maastricht Treaty left room for flexibility since it merely prohibits a trend of excessive deficits.
Consequently, Welteke said the trend, not the actual numbers, is critical, particularly as a nation's fiscal policies become more important once their individual currencies are molded into one.
"What is the critical difference between a budget deficit of 2.8 or 3.2 percent and who can really measure gross domestic product perfectly accurately at any given point in time?" Welteke said.
On the other hand Welteke, also president of the state central bank in Hesse, warned against opening the union to nations with lax fiscal policies.
"I do not think that any nation should be accepted which has not launched stability oriented policies," he said.

Asked to comment more specifically on Italy, Spain and Portugal's chances of being among the first group of nations to adopt the euro, Welteke gave a studiously neutral answer, steering clear of predictions but praising recent efforts.
